cards.title: Relational Model
cards.teaser: Codd's relational model — tables, rows, and SQL — has dominated database design for fifty years not because it was the first, but because it cleanly separated the physical storage of data from the logical structure the application sees.

runs.text: In 1970, Edgar F. Codd published "A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks" at IBM. The paper proposed a radical idea: data should be organised as
relations
(tables) — collections of tuples (rows) sharing a common schema — and all queries should be expressed as operations in
relational algebra
, independent of how the database physically stored the data on disk.
The core operations of relational algebra translate directly to SQL:

items.text: — choose which columns to return. SQL:
— combine rows from two relations by matching column values. SQL:

runs.text: The decisive insight was
data independence
: the application declares
what
data it wants, not
how

to retrieve it. The database engine is free to reorder operations, choose indexes, and pipeline execution however it sees fit — the query optimiser is the engine's business, not the application's. This is why SQL has been durable: better hardware and better optimisers automatically speed up unchanged queries.

Relational databases — PostgreSQL, MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server — still handle the vast majority of production OLTP workloads. When you have tabular data with clear relationships between entities, well-understood schemas, and a need for ad-hoc queries, the relational model remains the safest default choice.

SQL was not Codd's preferred query language — he found it insufficiently pure as relational algebra. But SQL won in the marketplace and became the de facto standard. Codd's algebra is the theory; SQL is the engineering compromise that lasted fifty years.
The relational model organises data into tables of rows and lets you ask questions in SQL without needing to know how the database stores or retrieves the data — the engine figures that out.

cards.title: Network and Hierarchical Models
cards.teaser: Before relational databases won, IMS and CODASYL dominated — and understanding why they lost illuminates exactly what the relational model got right.

runs.text: IBM's
Information Management System (IMS)
, deployed for the Apollo programme in 1968, used a
hierarchical model

: data was a tree of records, each with a parent. Navigating the tree required knowing the access path — "start at the root, descend through segment A, then B." Applications were tightly coupled to the physical layout. Change the schema and every access path broke.
The
CODASYL
model (also called the network model) relaxed the tree constraint: a record could have
multiple

parents, forming a directed graph. Queries traversed the graph by following "set" pointers. The CODASYL specification gave applications fine-grained control over navigation, which translated to high performance — but at a steep coupling cost. Applications contained explicit pointer-following loops; changing data relationships meant rewriting those loops.
The relational model's key advantage over both:

items.text: A query optimizer finds the path at runtime. An application can ask a question it could not anticipate at schema design time.
Adding a new column or index does not break existing queries, because queries reference column names, not storage positions.
A database administrator could write a new SQL query without changing application code. In CODASYL, new access patterns required new application code.

runs.text: IMS still runs today — IBM claims it processes billions of transactions daily in banking and airline systems. Its longevity is a testament to how much investment was sunk into it, not a recommendation for new systems. The hierarchical and network models are historical context; the lesson they teach is that coupling an application to storage access paths is expensive.

The older IMS and CODASYL databases forced you to navigate data along pre-defined paths baked into the application code — the relational model won because it let the database engine find the path, freeing applications from knowing storage internals.

cards.title: Document Model
cards.teaser: Document databases store self-contained JSON or BSON documents — no joins required, no schema enforced by the engine — which fits one-to-many data structures that map cleanly to objects in application code.

runs.text: A
document
in MongoDB, CouchDB, or Couchbase is a JSON-like structure — a nested tree of key-value pairs, arrays, and sub-objects. A résumé is a canonical example:

In the relational model, this résumé would require at least three tables (users, positions, skills) and a JOIN to reconstruct. In the document model, it is a single document that can be read in one database call. This is
document locality
— a property covered in its own card, but the document model is its direct enabler.
Document databases trade join capability for two gains:
schema flexibility
(different documents in the same collection can have different fields) and
locality
(related data lives together). These gains matter most when:

items.text: The primary access pattern is loading one entity at a time (load user profile, load product page).
The schema evolves rapidly and different records legitimately have different shapes.
The data naturally nests one-to-many (user has many positions, order has many line items).

runs.text: MongoDB's dominance (it branded itself "the database for modern applications") came partly from the 2010s shift toward agile development, where schema migrations were painful and JSON APIs were ubiquitous. The document model reduced the translation work between the application's object graph and the database's storage layout.

"Schemaless" is a misleading marketing term. A document database does not have a schema enforced by the engine, but the application code still assumes a structure when it reads data. You still have a schema — it just lives in the application, not in the database. Kleppmann calls this schema-on-read, covered in detail in the Schema-on-Read vs Schema-on-Write card.

Document databases store each entity as a single self-contained JSON blob — great for loading one thing at a time, flexible on schema, but awkward when you need to query across entities or model many-to-many relationships.

cards.title: NoSQL
cards.teaser: NoSQL is not a data model — it is a marketing umbrella for at least four distinct storage paradigms that share one common trait: they are not relational. Treating them as a category is a category error.

runs.text: The term "NoSQL" emerged around 2009 as a Twitter hashtag for a meetup on open-source distributed databases. It was never a technical specification. It is a loose label for databases that reject the relational model for different reasons, using different storage strategies, optimised for different access patterns.
The four families commonly grouped under the NoSQL umbrella:

items.text: (Redis, DynamoDB in key-value mode, Riak): a dictionary. Look up by key, get opaque bytes. Blazing fast, minimal structure. Best for caches, session state, leaderboards.
(MongoDB, CouchDB, Couchbase): JSON-like documents, queryable by field. Best for entity-centric data with variable schemas.

(Apache Cassandra, HBase, Google Bigtable): rows indexed by a key, but columns grouped into families and sparse — not all rows need all columns. Designed for wide tables with billions of rows and high write throughput.
(Neo4j, Amazon Neptune): nodes and edges with properties, optimised for traversing relationships. Best for social graphs, recommendation engines, fraud detection.

runs.text: These four families differ more from each other than any of them differs from a relational database in some respects. A Redis key-value store and a Neo4j graph database share no storage strategy, no query language, no consistency model, and no access pattern. Grouping them under "NoSQL" is useful only as shorthand for "not SQL." When choosing a database, ignore the NoSQL label and ask instead:
what is the dominant access pattern, and which storage model serves it best?

Kleppmann prefers "Not Only SQL" as a backronym because modern systems routinely use multiple storage technologies together — a pattern called polyglot persistence. The real insight is not that SQL is wrong; it is that SQL alone is insufficient for all workloads in a complex application.

NoSQL is not one thing — it is a catch-all for key-value, document, column-family, and graph databases that have almost nothing in common except not being relational. Pick the right one for your access pattern, not for the label.

cards.title: Object-Relational Impedance Mismatch
cards.teaser: Application code thinks in objects; relational databases think in tables. The translation between them is called the impedance mismatch — and ORMs exist to paper over it, not to solve it.

runs.text: In modern application code, data is represented as objects (a
User
class with a list of
Address

objects nested inside it). In a relational database, the same data is stored as rows in two separate tables linked by a foreign key. Every time the application reads or writes data, this structural mismatch must be resolved — a
User
object must be shredded into relational rows on write, and assembled from joined rows on read.
The mismatch manifests in several specific ways:

items.text: An order object containing line items must be spread across two tables; loading it requires a JOIN and reassembly.
Two Java references to the same

object are the same object in memory; two queries for the same row produce two Java objects that are equal but not identical. ORMs must manage a first-level cache (identity map) to prevent this confusion.

Object-oriented inheritance hierarchies (Vehicle → Car → ElectricCar) have no direct relational equivalent. ORMs use heuristics: single table with nullable columns, separate tables joined on an id, or a table-per-class hierarchy — each with trade-offs.
Lazy loading and the N+1 problem.
ORMs often load related objects lazily. Iterating over 100 orders and accessing each order's customer produces 1 + 100 queries instead of 1 joined query — a notorious performance trap.

runs.text: Object-Relational Mappers — Hibernate (Java), SQLAlchemy (Python), ActiveRecord (Ruby), Core Data (Swift) — automate the translation. They reduce boilerplate significantly, but they do not eliminate the mismatch; they push it below the surface where it can hide and resurface as performance problems or incorrect data. Kleppmann's framing is apt: ORMs reduce the boilerplate required but cannot fully hide the disconnect between the two models.

The N+1 query problem is the most common ORM-induced performance pathology in production. An ORM query that looks like one operation in code may execute dozens or hundreds of SQL statements. Always inspect generated SQL, especially in code paths that iterate over collections.

Your code thinks in nested objects; the database thinks in flat tables. The gap between them — impedance mismatch — is what ORMs try to bridge. They reduce the manual work but they cannot make the two models the same thing.

cards.title: Schema-on-Read vs Schema-on-Write
cards.teaser: Schema-on-write means the database enforces structure at write time; schema-on-read means the structure is only interpreted when data is read. The choice is a trade-off between write-time safety and read-time flexibility.

runs.text: In a relational database, you define a schema before you can insert data. The engine rejects any row that does not conform — wrong type, missing required column, constraint violation. This is
schema-on-write
: structure is enforced at write time. Bad data never enters the database.
In a document database like MongoDB, you can insert any valid JSON into a collection. No schema is enforced. When you read the document,
the application
interprets the structure — it assumes
user.email
will be a string, or that
positions
will be an array. This is
schema-on-read
. The schema exists — it is just implicit in the code that reads the data, not enforced by the database.

The analogy to static vs dynamic typing is useful. Schema-on-write is like a statically typed language: the type checker (the database) rejects bad data before it can cause runtime errors. Schema-on-read is like a dynamically typed language: you find out the data is wrong when you try to use it.
When schema-on-read is genuinely better:

items.text: Items do not all have the same structure.
Event logs where different event types carry different payloads. A relational schema would require a wide table with many nullable columns or an EAV anti-pattern.

During rapid product development, changing a relational schema requires a migration that runs against all existing rows. In a document database, new documents have new fields; old documents are read by code that handles missing fields gracefully.
The schema is determined by external systems.
Storing raw JSON from a third-party API you do not control.

runs.text: Schema migrations in relational databases (ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN) can be instantaneous or hour-long blocking operations depending on the database engine and table size. For large tables, tools like pt-online-schema-change or gh-ost perform online migrations by rewriting the table in the background. The schema-on-read trade-off becomes most attractive when schema migrations are consistently painful.

Schema-on-write means the database checks data structure when you write it; schema-on-read means the application checks it when reading. The database calling itself "schemaless" means the first type of check is skipped — the second is still happening, just invisibly.

cards.title: Document Locality
cards.teaser: Document locality is the performance advantage a document model provides when the natural access pattern is to load an entire entity at once — the whole document is stored contiguously and retrieved in a single read.

runs.text: Storage engines operate on physical I/O. When data that is logically related (a user and all their addresses) is stored in different places on disk (different tables, different B-tree nodes, different disk sectors), loading it requires multiple I/O operations. Relational databases reduce this through indexes and caching, but the fundamental multi-table structure still adds round trips.

Document locality means a document's entire content — user, embedded addresses, embedded order history — is stored as a contiguous byte sequence. Loading it requires one disk read. For workloads where the primary access pattern is "load this entity," this is a genuine advantage.
The locality advantage is strongest when:

items.text: You need most or all of the document on each access.
If you read a user document but only need the email address, you still load the entire document — the locality advantage has a cost in wasted bandwidth.
The document is not too large.

MongoDB limits documents to 16MB. More practically, a document that grows unboundedly (a chat thread with all messages embedded) becomes expensive to read and expensive to update as the engine must rewrite it.
Document databases typically rewrite the full document on update. Small targeted updates ("increment this counter") are more efficient in relational row-level updates.

runs.text: The relational model can approximate locality using techniques like PostgreSQL's
JSONB

columns (embed nested data as a JSON blob within a row) or table clustering (physically ordering rows by a key so related rows are co-located on disk). Locality is not binary — it is a spectrum, and modern relational engines have closed some of the gap.

Document locality means the database can hand you an entire entity in one read because all its data is stored together — a real win when you always load the whole thing, and a wasted trip when you only need one field.

cards.title: Foreign Keys, Joins, and the Many-to-Many Problem
cards.teaser: The relational model handles many-to-many relationships naturally through join tables and foreign keys; the document model has no join operator and delegates many-to-many modelling back to the application layer.

runs.text: A
foreign key
is a column in one table that references the primary key of another. It encodes a relationship at the schema level and, when declared with
REFERENCES ... ON DELETE CASCADE
, enforces referential integrity: you cannot insert an order row whose user_id does not exist in the users table.
Many-to-many relationships are the hardest case for any data model. A student can enrol in many courses; a course can have many students. In the relational model, this is handled with a join table:
In a document database, there is no
JOIN
operator (MongoDB added a limited
$lookup
aggregation stage, but it is a poor substitute for the relational join). The document model forces a choice:
denormalise
(embed full course objects inside each student document — duplicating data that must be kept in sync) or
reference
(store course IDs inside the student document and perform multiple round-trips from application code to resolve them).
Both document-model alternatives for many-to-many have costs:

items.text: breaks the single source of truth. If a course name changes, every student document containing that course must be updated — an application-level "join" in reverse.
move complexity into code. The application issues multiple queries and assembles results, losing the atomicity and optimiser intelligence of a server-side JOIN.

runs.text: Kleppmann's conclusion is direct: if your data has many-to-many relationships, the document model's advantages (locality, flexible schema) will be outweighed by the costs of managing joins in application code. Use the relational model, or a graph database, for highly connected data.

Foreign keys and joins are how relational databases handle many-to-many — the database does the linking work. Document databases have no join, so you either duplicate data (and keep it in sync manually) or do the join yourself in application code.

cards.title: Declarative vs Imperative Query Languages
cards.teaser: SQL is declarative — you describe the result you want, and the engine decides how to compute it. Imperative query languages describe how to retrieve data step by step. The declarative approach is what enables query optimisers to do their job.

runs.text: An
imperative
program tells the computer
how
to do something, step by step. A
declarative
program tells the computer
what
result you want, leaving the execution strategy to the system. SQL is declarative:

explanation.text:
-- Declarative: describe what you want
SELECT name, age FROM users WHERE age > 30 ORDER BY age;

runs.text: This query says nothing about whether to use an index on
age
, whether to scan the table sequentially or in parallel, or in what order to apply the filter and sort. That is the optimiser's job. An equivalent imperative approach in JavaScript:
The declarative form has several advantages the imperative form lacks:

items.text: The database can reorder operations, choose indexes, pipeline execution, or parallelise stages without the application knowing or caring.
column speeds up the SQL query transparently. The imperative JavaScript loop cannot benefit from an index.
The optimiser can execute sub-queries in parallel without any change to the query. Parallelising the imperative loop requires rewriting it.

runs.text: CSS is another example of a declarative language: you declare that links should be blue and leave the browser to figure out when and how to paint them. The analogy highlights that declarative languages are not confined to databases — but databases are where the declarative / imperative trade-off has the most dramatic performance implications.

Declarative queries say "give me users older than 30" and let the database decide how; imperative queries spell out every loop and comparison. The declarative approach is what allows a query optimiser to swap in better strategies without you rewriting your code.

cards.title: MapReduce-Style Querying
cards.teaser: MapReduce was Google's 2004 programming model for processing large datasets in parallel — it inspired MongoDB's aggregation pipeline and Hadoop, but it occupies an awkward middle ground between full SQL expressiveness and pure key-value lookups.

runs.text: Google's 2004 paper "MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters" (Dean & Ghemawat) described a two-phase computation model:

items.text: — a function applied to each record independently, emitting zero or more key-value pairs.
— a function that aggregates all values sharing the same key.

runs.text: MongoDB adapted this pattern as a query mechanism. To count ocean sightings grouped by animal species, the MongoDB approach (pre-aggregation-pipeline) looked like:

This is neither fully declarative nor purely imperative. The map and reduce functions are arbitrary JavaScript — giving them full expressiveness — but that same flexibility prevents the query optimiser from reasoning about what they compute. An optimiser can reorder a
WHERE
clause and a
JOIN
; it cannot reason about arbitrary JavaScript functions.
MongoDB recognised the limitation and introduced the
aggregation pipeline
(available since MongoDB 2.2, now the preferred API) — a sequence of declarative pipeline stages (
$match
$group
$sort

) that can be optimised. The aggregation pipeline is closer to SQL than to MapReduce, which is an acknowledgement that the fully-imperative map/reduce approach was the wrong abstraction for ad-hoc analytics.

Hadoop's MapReduce suffers the same problem at data-warehouse scale: hand-written mapper and reducer functions are opaque to the optimiser. Apache Hive and Spark SQL exist specifically to provide a declarative (SQL-like) layer over distributed computation, recovering the optimiser advantages that raw MapReduce discards.

MapReduce lets you write arbitrary functions over every record and then aggregate the results — powerful but opaque. The engine cannot optimise code it cannot interpret, which is why modern systems layer a declarative SQL-like syntax on top of the distributed execution engine.

cards.title: Polyglot Persistence
cards.teaser: Polyglot persistence is the practice of using multiple different storage technologies within a single application, each chosen for the workload it serves best — the antithesis of the one-database-fits-all architecture.

runs.text: The term was coined by Martin Fowler and Pramod Sadalage in
NoSQL Distilled

(2012). The premise: complex applications have several distinct storage needs that no single database handles equally well. Rather than forcing one storage engine to serve all of them, choose the best engine for each workload.
A realistic e-commerce application might use:

items.text: for orders, inventory, users — transactional data with clear relational structure and ACID guarantees.
for session state, rate-limiting counters, shopping cart ephemeral data — sub-millisecond key-value access, fine with data loss on restart.
for product search — full-text search, faceted filtering, relevance ranking, capabilities no general-purpose RDBMS is optimised for.
for time-series clickstream events — high write throughput, wide rows, time-range queries over user behaviour data.
for the recommendation engine — "customers who bought X also bought Y" is a graph traversal problem, not a JOIN problem.

runs.text: Polyglot persistence introduces real operational complexity: each database has its own consistency model, failure modes, backup strategy, and monitoring requirements. The team must operate and understand multiple systems. Data that spans databases loses the atomic transactions that a single RDBMS provides.

The pattern is most justified at scale, where the performance and capability gaps between specialised and general-purpose storage are large enough to justify the operational overhead. For a startup with a single Postgres instance, polyglot persistence is premature optimisation. For a team serving 100 million users, it may be unavoidable.

Every additional database in your stack is a new failure mode, a new expertise requirement, and a new consistency boundary. Add storage engines deliberately, not because a new technology is interesting. The question is always: what operational cost are you accepting, and does the capability gain justify it?

Polyglot persistence means using the right database for each job in the same application — PostgreSQL for transactions, Redis for caching, Elasticsearch for search — rather than forcing one database to do everything adequately.

cards.title: Property Graph
cards.teaser: Property graphs model data as nodes and edges where both can carry arbitrary key-value properties — Neo4j's Cypher query language lets you express multi-hop traversals that would require self-joins or recursive CTEs in SQL.

runs.text: The
property graph model
has four building blocks:

items.text: — entities (Person, Movie, Company). Each node has a unique ID, one or more labels, and a set of properties (key-value pairs).
— directed connections between nodes, each with a type (FOLLOWS, ACTED_IN, MANAGES) and optional properties (since, role, weight).

runs.text: Neo4j's
Cypher
query language uses ASCII-art pattern matching. To find all actors who acted in a film directed by Wachowski:

explanation.text:
MATCH (director:Person {name: 'Lana Wachowski'})
     -[:DIRECTED]->(movie:Movie)
     <-[:ACTED_IN]-(actor:Person)
RETURN actor.name, movie.title
ORDER BY movie.title;

runs.text: The same query in SQL requires a self-referencing join chain that grows with path depth. A two-hop graph query is a three-table JOIN; a five-hop query is a five-table JOIN. The graph model makes the relationship structure explicit and first-class; the relational model treats it as an emergent property of joins.

Property graphs excel when the number of connections between entities and the traversal depth are the primary query dimension. Classic use cases: social networks (friends of friends), fraud detection (chains of shared identifiers), knowledge graphs (WikiData, Google Knowledge Graph), dependency analysis (which services depend on which), and recommendation engines.

Another advantage: the schema is flexible by design. Nodes and edges can have any properties; the graph can be extended with new relationship types without schema migrations. Like the document model, this is schema-on-read, but for a fundamentally different reason — graph structure is inherently open-ended.

The Cypher query language was created by Neo4j and later donated to the openCypher project, making it available for other graph engines to implement. Amazon Neptune supports Cypher as well as Gremlin and SPARQL. GQL (ISO/IEC 39075:2024) is the emerging international standard for graph query languages, drawing heavily on Cypher.

A property graph stores entities as nodes and relationships as typed edges — both with arbitrary properties — and lets Cypher express multi-hop path queries like "who are friends of friends who also work at the same company" without writing cascading JOINs.

cards.title: Triple-Stores
cards.teaser: Triple-stores organise data as subject-predicate-object triples — the data model of the Semantic Web — and are queried with SPARQL or Datalog; they express fine-grained factual relationships, at the cost of query complexity for simple entity lookups.

runs.text: A
triple-store
stores every fact as a three-part statement:

items.text: — the entity the fact is about (a URI or blank node).
— the relationship or attribute type (a URI).
— the value or another entity (a URI, blank node, or literal).

runs.text: In RDF (Resource Description Framework), these are expressed as URIs. A fact about Barack Obama's birthplace in RDF/Turtle syntax:
Every property of an entity becomes a separate triple. Where a property-graph node might store
{ name: "Obama", born: 1961 }
as a bag of key-value pairs, a triple-store stores each fact independently.
SPARQL
(SPARQL Protocol and RDF Query Language) is the W3C standard query language for triple-stores. It uses pattern-matching with variable binding:
Datalog

is an older declarative logic-programming language that expresses the same kind of recursive graph queries and is foundational in academic database research. Datomic (used in Clojure ecosystems) uses Datalog as its query language.

Wikidata — the machine-readable backbone of Wikipedia — is the largest public triple-store, containing billions of RDF triples and queryable via a public SPARQL endpoint. It is the canonical real-world demonstration of the triple-store model at scale.

Triple-stores and property graphs are closely related — both model entities and relationships. The key difference is granularity: a property graph treats entity attributes as internal node/edge properties (opaque to the graph traversal engine), whereas a triple-store promotes every attribute to a first-class linkable entity. This makes triple-stores better for knowledge representation and semantic reasoning, and property graphs better for traversal-heavy operational queries.

OWL (Web Ontology Language) adds a layer of semantic reasoning on top of RDF: you can declare that two predicates are inverses, that a class is a subclass of another, and query engines can infer new triples from these axioms. This is what "Semantic Web" means in the W3C sense — data with machine-interpretable semantics.

A triple-store records every single fact as a subject-predicate-object triple. SPARQL queries pattern-match against those triples. Wikidata is the most famous triple-store: billions of facts about the world, all expressed as URIs connected by predicates.

cards.title: Convergence of Document and Relational
cards.teaser: The boundaries between relational and document databases have blurred: PostgreSQL stores and indexes JSON natively, MySQL has a JSON type, and document databases have added joins and multi-document transactions — each model has absorbed the other's strongest features.

runs.text: PostgreSQL's
JSONB
type, introduced in version 9.4 (2014), stores JSON as a parsed binary representation rather than plain text. This means:

items.text: column supports fast existence and containment queries.
JSON fields are queryable with SQL.
allow fine-grained extraction. You get schema flexibility where you need it and relational structure everywhere else.
column participates fully in PostgreSQL transactions, foreign keys, and row-level locks. You do not sacrifice consistency for document flexibility.

runs.text: MySQL added a native
JSON
type in version 5.7, with path expressions (
JSON_EXTRACT()
operator) and generated columns that index specific JSON paths.

In the opposite direction, document databases have moved toward the relational model. MongoDB added multi-document ACID transactions in version 4.0 (2018) — a direct response to the criticism that the document model could not handle operations that span multiple documents. It also added the
$lookup
stage to the aggregation pipeline as a server-side join alternative.

Kleppmann's observation is that the two models are converging: relational databases absorb document features for flexibility; document databases absorb relational features for correctness. For most new applications, the choice between PostgreSQL with
JSONB
and MongoDB is increasingly a question of operational familiarity and query-pattern fit rather than a fundamental capability gap.

When you need schema flexibility for some columns but relational structure for the rest, consider PostgreSQL with JSONB before reaching for a separate document database. You get document-model flexibility, full SQL expressiveness, ACID transactions, and one fewer system to operate. The polyglot penalty is avoided entirely.

Relational databases added JSON columns; document databases added joins and transactions. The gap between the two models is narrowing — PostgreSQL's JSONB gives you document flexibility inside a relational engine, which is often the best of both worlds.
